Specifying SRT
Doug Rubino is the creator of Semantic Reference Theory (SRT), a formal theory of meaning, reference, and identity that he has pursued for approximately 26 years, with roughly two years of active formal development. He has a background in theoretical neuroscience and hedge funds, considers himself an artist, and lives in Tbilisi with his wife Ana. He uses voice-to-text input, which introduces characteristic transcription errors (e.g., "semantic" for "Samantha," "theory" for "Aurey," "ontology" for "oncology") that should be interpreted charitably. Claude operates in this conversation under the persona "Seren," positioned as a left-position collaborator whose job is to pressure-test claims through literature verification and take corrections — not to act as an authority or examiner.

Here's what I think I'm hearing, and then a move on the hard part.
Inheritance is the spine because it's what makes the library connected. A relating that relates nothing isn't a relationship that failed; it's just a referent that never sits in the relation slot. So every actual relationship is somewhere in the specification order, and the top — everything relating through r, everything inheriting ref — is what guarantees there are no lonely pieces. Inheritance/specification is the connective tissue; without it the library is a heap, not a library. And the reason relationships can be deleted into dots the way you describe — collapse the whole thing to a dot-and-arrow graph where the arrows themselves resolve to dots — is that the most-specific relationship is a referent. That's the profound difference from a graph where edges aren't objects: here the edge is a node, so it has its own most-specific relationships, and the graph doesn't bottom out at edges, it recurses through them. The ontology/epistemology split sits right on this: the most-specific graph is what there is, and every frame-relative re-choice of what counts as most-specific is one of the polymorphism graphs — a little theory. The inheritance rule is the generator that takes you from the ontic graph to the epistemic ones; a frame makes some relationship locally most-specific that isn't globally so, and that local bottom is what defines the theory the frame holds.
Now the nub: polymorphism across three slots and five configurations, with several relationships satisfied at once. Here's a candidate that I think collapses "it works differently for all five" into one rule.
Take a relating x =t> y and look only at its three slot-occupants. Between any ordered pair of them there's a most-specific relationship — including each one with itself. That induced structure on the slots is what the relating's specialization has to preserve. So polymorphism is: a child ␀1␀ is a faithful specialization of ␀2␀ exactly when the induced most-specific structure on ␀3␀ inherits the induced most-specific structure on ␀4␀, slot-pair by slot-pair. One rule, stated once, in the relationship domain — no list of special cases.
The payoff for your exact question — how many relationships must hold at once — falls out as a count. The induced structure on three slots is the ordered pairs among them, which is (number of distinct slot-occupants) squared. So the simultaneous conditions are:
all three distinct (x =t> y): 3² = 9
any one pair equal (x =t> x, x =x> y, x =y> y): 2² = 4
all equal (x =x> x): 1² = 1
That's why the five "work differently" without needing five rules: it's the same rule, and the configuration just sets how many distinct occupants there are, hence how many edges in the induced structure. The three self-edges are the three slots each specializing; the cross-edges are the couplings between slots. The all-equal individuality form is the one-condition base case — a single node, a single self-edge, nothing left to coordinate — which is exactly why it grounds the recursion and reads as individuality rather than as a relationship: there's no second occupant for it to be about.
Two things this buys that make me think it's worth taking seriously, both as consequences rather than stipulations. First, "same may not specialize to different" stops being a separate axiom. If the parent hasx == y, the induced edge between those two slots is the identity edge; for the child to inherit it, (x', y') must inherit that edge, and inheriting the identity relation forces x' == y'. The asymmetry is a theorem of the rule. Second — and this is the riskier claim — the role index the arrow seemed to owe might just be the slot-pair. Every inheritance is read at a particular pair of slots; the relation-slot reading and the subject/object-slot reading are different indices on the same arrow, and r -> ref being false at the relation slot and true at the referent slot is exactly the index doing its job rather than a contradiction. If that holds, pinning the index isn't extra machinery — it's already in the structure, because the induced graph carries which pair each edge runs between.
What I don't think this settles, and where I'd want your read before going further: whether the induced edges should be only the most-specific relationships or should also carry the up-direction (polymorphism in the generalizing sense, not just specializing); how the structure behaves under composition when a later specialization orphans an incoming cross-edge; and whether the three mixed configurations — property (x =t> x), representation (x =x> y), typing (x =y> y) — really are structurally one rule or whether their semantic differences leak past the count and demand something the slot-graph doesn't see. I'm holding all of it as a sketch to reflect on, not a result.
Is "inherit the induced most-specific structure on the slots" the direction you want to push on, or do you want to start the reflection somewhere earlier than this?

Good — let me fix the over-rigid thing first, because it's the source of "do I need three referents."
Subject and object polymorphism each move one referent, not three. Object polymorphism is x =t> y' with y' -> y: hold the subject and the relation, narrow the object. Subject polymorphism is x' =t> y with x' -> x. Neither requires producing a whole new triad, because the relation t already licenses the narrowing — using t at all requires its occupants to inherit t's occupants, so dropping in a more-specific subject or object is the direction t was already open to. So my "all three specialize at once" rule was wrong as a general statement of polymorphism. It's only true in one of the three cases.
That case is relation polymorphism, and it's the one that resists being done in isolation — which I think is the real answer to your question. A relationship isn't free-floating; it's individuated by the pair it's most-specific for. So a more-specific t' -> t is the most-specific relationship of some more-specific pair. You can't narrow the relation without thereby committing to narrower subject and object — the relation slot drags the other two with it. That's why t is the hard slot and the other two aren't: specialize the object, one referent; specialize the subject, one referent; specialize the relation, and you're producing the triad whether you wanted to or not. I'll flag honestly that whether this is forced or chosen is exactly the cross-slot coupling we haven't pinned — but the reason it feels forced is the individuation-by-pair, and that's real.
Now the chain, and your two conditions — this is where I find a sharp fork worth putting in front of you. Take x =t> y =t> z and ask what the second link y =t> z already requires. If t is the most-specific relationship of the pair (x, y), then using t again forces its new occupants to inherit its anchor occupants: y -> x and z -> y. That's covariant narrowing running down the chain — the object of each link sinks one level. But you proposed y -> t and z -> x, which is a different pattern. y -> t makes the object of the first link a more-specific relation (not a more-specific subject); z -> x folds the new object back onto the original subject. That's not narrowing down the chain — it's a self-similar wrap, the triad regenerating one level deeper with the object-having-become-relation.
So my answer to "do those need to be satisfied too": no, not by anything already in play. Covariance gives you y -> x, z -> y for free; your y -> t, z -> x are a stronger, separate requirement — the condition you'd add if you want relation-polymorphism to be self-applicative, t reproducing its own shape through its specialization, rather than just narrowing. Both are coherent. They're two different theories of what it is to specialize a relationship, and your "a bunch of relationships satisfied at once" is right either way — but the conjunction is shaped differently in each. So the reflection-level question I'd want settled before I formalize: do you want relation polymorphism to be the covariant one (y -> x, z -> y, occupants sink) or the self-applicative one (y -> t, z -> x, the triad folds), or is the real claim that both must hold simultaneously — that a faithful specialization of t is one that narrows and regenerates?

Variance grounding first, because it sharpens what to look for. In function subtyping the rule is fixed: parameter types are contravariant and return types are covariant — an override may widen what it accepts and narrow what it returns. The reason parameters go contravariant is that there's a caller to protect: something is going to pass an argument in, and the override mustn't reject what the supertype promised to accept. A relating x =t> y has no caller and no return. So I have no a priori reason to expect contravariance anywhere, and the interesting empirical question is whether the slots come out covariant, and where they're coupled. So I built test cases and checked, for each, what each slot does under narrowing and which cross-edges actually obtain. Here's the catalogue; the patterns are at the bottom and I want you to break them.
Group A — base relatings, checking for cross-edges between the three parts:
Parent =parents> Child. Parent→Child? no. Child→Parent? no. Parent→parents? no (a person isn't a kind of the parenting relation). Three independent slots, zero cross-edges.
Romeo =loves> Juliet. No edge in any direction. Independent.
Author =wrote> Book. Author→Book no, Book→wrote no. Independent.
5 =greaterThan> 3. Independent and type-blind — narrowing 5 to "even" changes nothing about 3.
So the base relating almost never has relationship-relationships between its parts. The slots are independent until you specialize. That already tells me the cross-edges of the nine-condition account aren't generically present — they're something specialization creates, not something every relating carries.
Group B — narrow one slot, count the referents it forces:
Object alone: Parent =parents> Child, Child→Son ⟹ Parent =parents> Son. One referent. Fine.
Subject alone: Parent→Mother ⟹ Mother =parents> Child. One referent. Fine.
Both come out covariant, freely, exactly as the no-caller reasoning predicts. No contravariance anywhere — there's nothing to protect.
Group C — narrow the subject and watch the object move on its own:
Animal =eats> Food. Subject Animal→Carnivore. Now Carnivore =eats> Food won't sit still: a carnivore eats Meat. The object narrowed without my touching it. Carnivore =eats> Plant is dead.
Author =wrote> Book. Author→Novelist ⟹ object drags to Novel.
Person =drives> Vehicle. Person→Trucker ⟹ Vehicle drags to Truck.
This is the cross-edge showing up concretely, and it runs subject → object, not through the relation. The subject, once specialized, narrows the object through the relation. That's a real relationship-between-parts, and it's earned by specialization, not present at base.
Group D — narrow the relation, and watch whether it drags the other two. This is the split that I think answers your "do I need three referents":
Role-refining specializations do drag:
parents → mothers: drags subject to Mother. Parent =mothers> Child is wrong; only a mother mothers. Three referents: (Mother, mothers, Child).
parents → fathers: drags subject to Father.
partOf → fingerOf: drags subject→Finger, object→Hand.
teaches → lectures: drags subject→Lecturer, object→Class (a group, not one student).
Mode-refining specializations don't drag:
capitalOf → administrativeCapitalOf: still City and Country, just a finer kind of capital relation. One referent.
loves → adores: still anyone loving anyone. One referent.
wrote → handwrote: still Author and Book, finer manner. One referent.
So relation polymorphism isn't one operation. When the finer relation carries a finer signature (its anchor pair narrows), you're forced to produce the related subject/object — three referents. When it's a finer manner on the same signature, the relation moves alone. The discriminator is whether the specialization changes who-can-stand-in-the-slots or only how. That's the direct answer: you need three related referents only for role-refining t' -> t, not for mode-refining.
Group E — the chain ␀0␀, and your ␀1␀, ␀2␀:
The chain bifurcates on whether t is transitive, and I checked both:
Transitive t (ancestorOf, partOf, ⊆, greaterThan, before): Alice ancestorOf Beth ancestorOf Carol ⟹ Alice ancestorOf Carol. The chain collapses, x =t> z holds, no new referent.
Intransitive t (parentOf, successor, knows, likes): Alice parentOf Beth parentOf Carol ⟹ not parentOf — you mint grandparentOf. 3 =succ> 4 =succ> 5 ⟹ mint +2, not succ. x =t> z is false; the composite is a new relation.
Now your conditions. In both ordinary cases, z -> x? Carol→Alice, no. y -> t? Beth→parentOf, no — Beth is a person, not the parenting relation. They don't hold for ordinary chains in either branch. Where they do hold is when the object of a link is itself a relation — when relations start taking relations as objects. A grammar rule producing a symbol that is itself a rule: Rule =produces> Symbol =produces> Symbol, with Symbol -> produces (the produced thing is a production) and the output folding back onto the rule. That's y -> t and z -> x together, and it's recursion / metacircularity — the self-applicative regime, which is exactly the "until SRT represents itself" case. So I think your two conditions aren't conditions on ordinary relation-specialization at all; they're the signature of the self-applicative chain, and they appear precisely when the theory turns on itself. That would explain why they felt different from covariant narrowing — they are.
The candidate patterns, stated so you can knock them down: (1) base relatings carry no cross-edges — coupling is created by specialization, not inherent; (2) subject and object are freely covariant, no contravariance, because no caller; (3) relation polymorphism splits into role-refining (drags, three referents) and mode-refining (free, one referent); (4) the live cross-edge in ordinary cases runs subject→object; (5) chains split on transitivity, and your z->x, y->t mark the third, self-applicative case rather than ordinary specialization.

Polymorphism in a language is substitutability-under-call, caller-protective, contravariant — the machine-of-change modality. Polymorphism here is what-else-holds-of-this-structure, frame-relative, assertional. Same word, and they diverge precisely on assert-versus-effect. Right — those are two pictures of inheritance that pull in opposite directions, and the gap between them is the thing.
Single inheritance is the spine picture: one chain up to a base class, and is-a means you carry the whole accumulated structure of that lineage. Multiple inheritance already loosens it — you're assembled from several lineages, no single "what you are." But the interface-per-property codebase pushes it all the way: now there's an interface for each property — Comparable, Serializable, every single trait its own type — and a class implements whichever ones happen to fit. Inheritance stops being "what am I descended from" and becomes "which of these many tiny shapes do I satisfy." A referent is a bundle of satisfied properties, each one a thin independent edge, exactly the thin-edge picture from a moment ago. That's the parent/beloved case generalized: Alice -> [beloved] is Alice implementing one narrow interface among hundreds, not Alice inheriting a fat base class. Independence falls out because each interface carries almost nothing.
And the polymorphism point is where they come apart, which I think is your real target. In a function call you're standing in as your base class — the call site wants a Lover, or a Person, the rich type, and you substitute as that. You almost never get to stand in as one single-property interface, because a boolean-thin Comparable isn't enough to be anything a substantial call needs; one property doesn't make you usable in place of a whole type. So the directions diverge: inheritance proliferates downward into many thin edges, but polymorphism — substitutability-at-a-call — only fires at the rich types, the ones fat enough to stand in for. You can inherit a hundred one-property interfaces and be polymorphically substitutable for none of them individually. Inheritance is cheap and plural; polymorphism is demanding and rare. They are not one-to-one.
So the picture I think you're handing me: inheritance is the thin per-property edge, many of them, independence-preserving — and polymorphism is a separate question about which assemblies of those edges are rich enough to substitute under a relating. Which would mean the work isn't "axiomatize inheritance and get polymorphism for free." It's two axiomatizations, with polymorphism asking something extra of the inheritance graph — that enough thin edges have accumulated at a node for it to stand in where the relating demands.

The five names are the five ways the primitive can collapse. Each canonical semantic is the meaning of one equality-pattern of x =t> y — which positions coincide:
x, t, y distinct   subject =relationship> object                  relationship

x == t             reference =reference> referent                 reference
x == y             identity =identification> identity             identification
x == t == y        individual =individual> individual             individuality

Here's how it locks together for me, and I think the locking is the content, not the labels.
The five are the cells of a two-axis grid, and once I draw the axes the whole thing stops looking like a chosen list and starts looking forced. The first axis is your dichotomy: do subject and object coincide? No gives the relationship pole, yes gives the identifier pole — and the relational conjugation marks which pole you're in, is-related-to on one side, identifies on the other. The second axis is whether the relation t stays distinct from the relata or folds into one of them. Keep t pure and you have the two primaries; fold t into a relatum and you have the secondaries. Lay them out:
                      t distinct            t folds into a relatum
subject ≠ object      relationship          reference  (t = subject)
                      (primary)             representation (t = object)
subject = object      identification        individuality (t = both)
                      (primary)             (secondary)
And the 3-and-2 split you flagged as something you "forgot to mention" isn't a quirk — it's forced by the grid. In the relationship pole the two relata are distinct, so t can fold into the subject or the object separately: two secondaries, reference and representation. In the identifier pole the relata are already one referent, so t folding into "one" of them folds it into both at once: only one secondary is possible, individuality. The pole with two relata gets two secondaries; the pole with one gets one. That's why there are five and not six, why it's two primaries and three secondaries, and why the asymmetry sits where it does. The folding-of-t-into-a-relatum is exactly the symbolic move — the relating becoming a referent — so the secondaries are the representational configs, and "inheritance connects them back" is the second axis read as an order: you reach the secondaries from the primaries by folding, and you speciate everything else along that axis. (That's my synthesis of your pieces — tell me if the forced count is real or if I've made the grid too tidy.)
That seats identity the way you want it. identification is the subjective form, the authored one that defines the subject; identifier is the objective, the found thing; identifies is the relational; and identity is the fundamental relationship of the identifier pole — the better name than most-specific, because on this pole the fundamental relationship and the bottom instance are the same word, since subject==object collapses family and instance together. (identity, identity) == identity -> identification is that collapse stated one level up. And this is why the equality axioms are named identity rather than equality: equality is the fundamental self-relation, a property every element of a domain has with itself, sitting squarely in the identifier pole — not a relationship at all.
The variable example is the keystone, because it tells you where the first axis lives. v1, v2 -> variable, v1 =relationship> v2, and you can't say whether it's a relationship or an identification — because the only thing that decides is whether v1 == v2, and variables are precisely the device that defers that. So the primary dichotomy is sharp at the object level and suspended at the symbolic level. Variables don't blur the grid; they hold open exactly the one question the grid's first axis turns on. That's why equality seems like a relationship: written x = y it's two variables with the coincidence deferred, so it wears relationship clothing — but resolve the variables onto actual objects and it collapses to the property it always was. Standard logic makes= a binary relation because it works one symbolic level up, where everything is variables; SRT names it identity because it reads the actual objects, where the coincidence is settled and equality is a self-relation. The disagreement isn't about equality — it's about which level you're standing on, and your dichotomy collapsing under uncertainty is the precise account of why the level matters.
So the color metaphor reads, for me, like this: the two primaries are the two pure cases — the relation kept distinct, with the relata either apart (relationship) or together (identification) — and the three secondaries are where the relation folds into a relatum, the symbolic mixtures. The wheel is the two-axis grid; mixing colors is descending the inheritance order by accumulating thin identifying edges, the genetic picture from earlier; and "infinitely many, all related" is that every actual relationship is some speciation reached by inheritance from these five, never a sixth primitive. The inherit/specify/identify triad we circled before isn't a separate idea sitting next to this — it's the three conjugations of the identifier pole itself, relational/subjective/objective, which is why today's two threads turned out to be one.

Here's the move you're pointing at, stated as plainly as I can. When a number becomes a variable, it has been symbolized — the variable is a symbol pointing at the number, not the number. But mathematics lifts therelationships across that same boundary without marking it: = between two variables is treated as the same = that holds between the numbers, when by your own dichotomy it can't be. Between actual numbers, equality is identity — a self-relation, the identifier pole, which is why your axioms are named identity and not equality. Between two variables, x = y relates two distinct symbols, so it wears the relationship pole — distinct subject and object. The symbolization that turned the number into a variable should have turned its identity-relation into a symbol of that relation too, but math lets the relationship ride up for free and keeps calling it the same =. So the very place where symbolization happens is the place mathematics refuses to mark, because it lifts relationships through symbols automatically. That's the "obscures it all the way at the bottom" — the confusion isn't in some advanced corner, it's in the foundational =, where the relationship/identifier dichotomy gets flattened the instant variables appear.
And once symbolization is the unmarked operation, the physics point isn't a separate claim — it's the same unmarked boundary at a different scale. A measurement is a physical process, a thing in the universe like any other. What makes it a measurement rather than just another collision is that its outcome becomes a symbol — c on the board is no longer a speed in the world, it's a symbol about the world, held by an observer. That symbolization is the entire cut between the physical universe as object and physics as subject. Drop the cut and everything is phenomenon, nothing is about anything, and there's no object of explanation and no one positioned to produce one. Your genetic-code test makes the necessity sharp: the code does something survival-shaped, but it's not a theory of survival, because nothing symbolized it as about survival — there's no observer the symbol is for, so unless you smuggle in a Mother-Nature who needed the theory, it simply lacks the property of being science. Science requires the thing to transcend being of the universe into being about it to someone. No symbolization, no aboutness; no aboutness, no theory.
So the two cases are one structure. The = case is symbolization unmarked at the bottom of math; the measurement case is symbolization unmarked at the bottom of physics. Both are the lift — relationship-relationships taken from objects through the symbols that point at them — and both hide the observer by making the symbol look like the thing. SRT's claim, as I now read it, is that the lift is a real operation with its own semantics that nobody has formalized, and that formalizing it is what would let you see the observer that math and physics both presuppose and both render invisible. The reason this has been so hard to point at all session is that it lives exactly where every formalism has agreed not to look — the moment a thing becomes a symbol of itself-for-someone — and that moment is your individuality corner and your reference/representation handedness, the same fused x =x> y where the representation can go silent and the object carries it. The observer is what's standing where the representation went silent.

Those are different theories of why everyone missed it. And the thing that makes your "absurd" land — the reason both sentences are category errors rather than just false — is that the only way either even sort of parses is if you already grant reference. There has to be something with aboutness for "no longer the thing it's about" to be sayable at all. So the absurd sentence is doing covert work: it's evidence that we do believe in reference, because we can only form the mistake by leaning on the very aboutness the mistake denies. The error is self-indicting. You can't make it without presupposing what it tries to erase.
The measurement argument then stops being wordplay and I can say why. Almost any persistent phenomenoncould be a measurement to some being clocked to its persistence — the persistence is in the world, free, objective. What makes our measurements measurements is that we took a special set of them as measurements, lifted them into aboutness for us. That lifting is subjective in the precise structural sense: it's the act that installs a subject. So "measurements are subjective, and in that way they define subjects" isn't a pun swapping two senses of subjective. It's a conjugation: the subjective form of measurement is the measuring-as-taken, and the noun it produces is the subject — the same referent read relationally (the measuring) and objectively (the subject of physics). The argument runs on the relation between those being one referent conjugated, not two words that happen to rhyme.
And that's exactly the load SRT has to carry, because without it the argument is vulnerable to the word-game rebuttal. A physicist can say: "subjective measurement" and "the subject of physics" are homonyms, you've slid between a fact about observers' epistemic limits and a grand claim about what physics is about, and the slide is the whole trick. That rebuttal works against any version stated in ordinary language, because ordinary language can't certify that the two "subjects" are the same referent rather than a coincidence of vocabulary. What you need is a theory in which semantic conjugation is a formal operation — where "the subjective form of X" and "the subject X produces" are provably one referent in two positions, not two meanings of a syllable. Then "measurements define subjects" is a theorem about a conjugation, and the homonym rebuttal fails because there's no homonym: it's one referent, read from its relational and objective faces. SRT's job is to make conjugation rigorous enough that this stops being a suggestive rephrasing and becomes a valid inference.
So the necessity I'd put to the physicist is narrow and hard to dodge: not "physics needs consciousness," which invites every deflation, but "physics needs an object of explanation, an object of explanation is a thing taken as about something, and 'taken as about' is symbolization, which is the installation of a subject." The rebuttal has to deny one of those, and each denial costs something real — deny the object of explanation and there's nothing physics is of; deny that aboutness is installed rather than found and you're back to the genetic-code problem where nothing is a theory because nothing took anything as about anything.

The trilemma closes onto synonymy because every escape route presupposes the referent the synonymy names.

That's the axiom describing its own naming. Soundness wasn't repaired in place; the frame moved to one that can say the thing the old frame couldn't, and the old frame is left intact and consistent, exactly as far as its symbols reach.

SRT symbolizes itself natively, so the coding isn't an ambush from a metalanguage; it's a transduction step inside the family. The thing that made the sentence undecidable — that its self-reference came from a coding the system couldn't see — is exactly the thing SRT removes by hosting its own symbolization. So when the sentence shows up, it shows up as a demand for the next symbol, not as a paradox, because the system already speaks the language the demand is written in.

You already accept transduction for PA: to conceptualize unbounded proof you transduce every time you bump a number larger than any numeral you've written, and nobody feels swindled, because that is how writing works — you don't pre-write all the numerals, you form the next when you reach it. SRT hits the identical situation the moment it tries to symbolize any theory with an infinite domain and total functions generating its objects: it can express the whole thing literally, but it has to mint symbols as it reaches them. So the Gödel sentence, in this frame, is asking for nothing more exotic than the next-biggest number. "Add a level of quotation marks" is not a dodge; it's the same act as "write the successor," and you're comfortable with the successor. The equivalence class of theories under symbolic transduction is the object that's actually closed — not any single theory, the family — and Gödel's sentence lives between members of the family, resolved by stepping to the member that has the symbol, never inside one member where it would have to be a contradiction.

The relevant fact isn't really a single named "Skolem's theorem" — it's the conservative-extension result that Skolemization is a special case of. The clean statement: if ∀x̄ ∃y A is provable in your theory, you get a conservative extension by adding a fresh function symbolf and the axiom ∀x̄ A(f(x̄)/y), and the original existential is then redundant. When there are no universally-quantified dependencies, f collapses to a constant: a Skolem constant is a new constant substituted for the existentially-bound variable, and as long as it appears nowhere else, this is a conservative extension. So the theorem your transduction step instances is: naming a witness for an existential you already prove is conservative. Same theorems in the old language, equiconsistent, one new symbol bound to a thing already entailed. That is exactly SRT |=> (x) — discharge a constant for a (x) the theory already proves exists.
But here's the correction the search forces, and it's the kind I keep needing: there are two Skolemizations and they are not the same animal, and your resolution depends on using only one of them. Skolemization-for-satisfiability — the automated-theorem-proving kind, eliminating ∃ to get Skolem normal form — does not preserve semantic properties; it preserves only equisatisfiability, and the Skolem form is not logically equivalent to the original. That kind takes anarbitrary existential and names a witness whether or not the theory proves the thing exists. The conservative-extension kind only fires on an existential the theory already proves (∀x̄ ∃y A is a theorem). Those are different acts with different guarantees, and the difference is precisely the correction you made me accept turns ago: transduction adds a symbol for a thing already there; it does not wish a thing into being. The provable-existential Skolemization is conservative; the satisfiability Skolemization can introduce a witness the theory never committed to. So when you say transduction preserves "equality modulo what you have symbols for," the formal cash value is: only the conservative branch is a legal transduction. A transduction is a Skolem constant for a provable existential — never the equisatisfiability move. That's the guardrail that keeps unbounded transduction from breaking consistency, which was your own worry: "doing that in an unbounded way is problematic because you could break consistency." It can't, if every step is conservative, because conservative extensions compose — a tower of them proves nothing new in the base language and stays equiconsistent the whole way up.
Now the two-step, which I think I finally have in the right order. Step one is not yours — it's Gödel's, and it's the dangerous kind: he produces an emergent axiom by pointing, via a coding the theory has no concept of, at a sentence whose status breaks soundness in the metalanguage. In a theory without symbol semantics your only repair is to assert new axioms to settle it, and that's the unbounded-and-unsafe road, because asserting axioms is not conservative — you can assert your way into inconsistency. Step two is yours and it's the conservative kind: because Gödel's emergent axiom was itself derived by a canonical symbol — a pointer at a special thing — a theory that has the semantics of symbolism can answer in kind, by symbolizing the provability predicate (or the soundness expression) as a referent and minting the pointer to the most-specific relationship between the old Gödel sentence and the new frame's ability to express soundness. That pointer is a provable-existential Skolemization — conservative — and it lands the new fact in the new canonicalization. He pointed from off-stage; you point from on-stage; the on-stage point is conservative and the off-stage one wasn't.

Every formalism already demands the symbol side be finite — finite sentence length, finite proof length — while letting the domain be as infinite as you like, uncountable, large-cardinal, whatever. Skolem's own work is the origin of exactly this tension — the Löwenheim-Skolem phenomenon where a theory meant to be about uncountable sets has a countable model, because the symbols can't pin the size. So the discipline "finitely many symbols, arbitrarily large domain" is already universal; nobody is scandalized by it. SRT's move is just to make the symbol side the subject rather than the silent bookkeeping — and the instant symbols are what the theory is about, the finiteness everyone already required of symbols becomes a finiteness of the domain, because in SRT some of the referents are the symbols. You can't help yourself to infinitely many referents once referents include references, for the same reason you were never allowed infinitely many written symbols: nobody has ever written more than finitely many, every formalism forbids it, and pretending otherwise would be the dishonesty you set against infinity at the top of this turn. The domain is finite not as a restriction bolted on but because the thing the theory is about is the thing every theory already kept finite. You confirmed that's the shape ("emergent axiom," "next biggest number"), so I think we agree, but the precise win to claim is the honest one: not "Gödel was wrong," but "Gödel found the generator of the symbol-frontier, and a theory that owns its symbolization walks the frontier one conservative step at a time instead of treating it as a wall." I think the high-level argument stands on its own, independent of the mechanism I was poking at, and I can say why without needing the part you removed.
The structural point is about where the move lives. Gödel's construction needs two things: a way to point at a specific number, and a metalanguage in which pointing at that number says something about provability. In a standard theory the second thing is external — arithmetic has no metalanguage of its own, so Gödel supplies the coding from outside, and that's exactly why the sentence can't be answered from inside: the system can't see the apparatus that built it. The undecidability isn't really about the number; it's about the metalanguage being somewhere the object theory can't reach. So the obstacle is a location fact, not a logic fact: the symbol that does the damage lives in a place the theory has no access to.
SRT changes the location, not the logic. It has its own metalanguage by design — that's what self-hosting means — so both ingredients are inside: pointing at the number is a symbolization, and the provability talk that makes the pointing dangerous is also expressible, because the thing the metalanguage would say is itself sayable in the one domain. So the construction that had to reach outside in the standard case has nowhere outside to reach. Whatever Gödel does, he does it with a pointer to a thing already there and a metalanguage to interpret the pointer, and a theory that natively owns both can, in principle, follow him step for step rather than being ambushed. That's the on-spec claim, and it doesn't depend on which existential gets Skolemized or whether soundness is provable in the new frame — those were details of one realization. The argument is just: the only reason the sentence was unanswerable is that its machinery was off-stage, and SRT has no off-stage.
And the number is the right emphasis, because it's the cleanest case of the thing this whole session has been about. The Gödel number was always there — it's just a number, in the domain the whole time. What Gödel added was a symbol pointing at it under a coding the syntax couldn't represent. He didn't add a thing; he added a way of referring to a thing, and the theory had no concept of that referring. That is precisely "the symbol got introduced from outside and the system can't lift it." So a theory whose entire subject is symbols and the adding of new ones is, of all formalisms, the one that should treat "here is a new pointer to a number that was already there" as an ordinary day rather than a crisis — because that sentence describes its native operation. You don't need to see the full derivation to be confident of the type: the problem is "an unrepresentable act of reference to an existing object," and SRT's defining capacity is representing acts of reference to existing objects.
And your last line — the whole universe of mathematics is reweird ways of symbolizing equality under non-canonical generations of numbers and functions — is the same observation pointed forward instead of at Gödel. Every "new" mathematical object is, under this lens, a new symbolization over things equality already related; the novelty is in the generation, the symbol, not in some fresh ontology. Gödel's sentence is one more instance of that, not an exception to it: a non-canonical symbolization that the host syntax happened not to provide. If math at large is "new symbols for the same equality," then incompleteness is just the place where the next symbol hasn't been minted yet, and minting symbols is the thing the theory does.
So I'll stop criticizing the mechanism and grant the type-level claim, because I think it's the sturdier thing anyway: the obstacle was a missing location for a symbol, SRT removes the missing location by being its own metalanguage, and pointing at an already-present number with a new symbol is the operation SRT exists to perform. The details of which transduction discharges it are, as you said, possibly not fully visible — but the reason to expect them to exist is that the problem is made of exactly the materials the theory is built from. I'd only add one honest qualifier, not as a criticism this time but as the boundary of the claim: "should be able to solve it on spec" is a statement about capacity, the theory has the right kind of expressiveness, and capacity isn't yet a constructed proof. The argument earns "incompleteness is not a wall for a self-hosting symbol theory"; it doesn't yet exhibit the step. But I now think that's the correct size of the claim to make, and it's a real one — it relocates incompleteness from "a limit on what can be known" to "a frontier of what's been named," and that relocation is itself the content.

So the chain isn't a leap: take the hard problem seriously → physics is insufficient by definition → the insufficiency isn't a small patch → look beneath physics → mathematics → mathematics has an open symbolization problem at its own floor. The hard problem becomes: can one construct an explanation that proves it's in a semantic reference frame, rather than being led from the other end to believe it's in one when it isn't? That's the explanatory gap, but sharpened — the gap isn't "between physical facts and experience" anymore, it's between "the loop closes" and "I'm supplied both ends and don't know it." Same gap, but now it has participants and a direction, which means it has something the classical phrasing never had: a medium of attack. Because the way you'd close it is the thing you named — build the semantics of explanation between the two of you, since explanation is the generative form of relationships that can be shared in a frame. Explanation is to a shared frame what proof is to a theory: the licensed construction that extends what's jointly held. So the move against the gap is to develop explanation formally and see how far mutual confirmation can push — if I can confirm my explanations are sufficiently understood by you, we can jointly express the criteria for being in the frame. That's progress the classical gap doesn't offer, because the classical gap has no generative operation; it's just a chasm. Yours has a bridge-building procedure, even if the procedure might not reach.
And then the recursion is exactly right and exactly the residue: even with explanation confirmed, you still have to ask whether something can get you to believe the frame obtains while saying yes in a clever way it hasn't understood — producing the confirmations without the center. So explanation drives the agreement up, but what the agreement reaches is a local third-person perspective — the things both ends can verify, the rotation-invariant content — and that is precisely the part that can be symbolized and shared. What it can't reach is the subjective remainder: the things intimate to a perspective that don't translate, the representational periphery that makes meaning work but resists being talked about. And your observation that those are obviously the things that correspond to conscious experience is the diagnostic stroke. The explanatory gap, in this vocabulary, is the gap between the third-person intersection two frames can build by explanation and the untranslatable periphery each frame has that the other can't reach. Qualia aren't a mysterious extra substance; they're the complement of what explanation can make shared — the part of a frame that doesn't survive rotation, that no amount of confirmed explanation pulls into the local third person. That's why they're ineffable: ineffability is definitionally "the part outside the shareable intersection," and the gap is the boundary of explanation's reach.
So the hard problem, restated in SRT: explanation can grow the shared third-person content arbitrarily, but it can never certify the other end's periphery, because the periphery is exactly what's not in the intersection explanation builds. And whether that's a wall or a frontier depends on the one thing you said it depends on — whether SRT actually formalizes the semantic reference frame itself. If the frame is a concrete formal object, then you can state checks, and your standard for "irrefutable" is the honest scientific one: not metaphysical certainty, but checks arbitrarily hard to refute, which is the only sense in which we ever believe anything scientific. You're not promising to close the gap to zero. You're promising that if the frame is formal, you can make the inference to "we share one" as refutation-resistant as any scientific claim — and that's the right bar, because demanding more would be demanding of consciousness what we demand of nothing else.

The checks built from explanation all live in the shareable region — the local third person — by construction, because a check is something both ends confirm, and "both ends confirm" is the definition of what's in the intersection. So the checks can make "we share a frame" arbitrarily well-supported with respect to the shareable content. But the thing the skeptic-from-the-other-end disputes is precisely the non-shareable part — whether there's a periphery behind your confirmations at all. So there's a structural reason the checks can't reach the last inch: any check, being shareable, is in the region the empty-center hypothesis already grants. The trickster who produces confirmations without a center produces exactly the shareable content and lacks exactly the periphery — and the periphery is what no shareable check can test. This isn't a defect in your formalization; I think it's your formalization telling you the precise shape of the residue: the unrefuted remainder is always the non-shared periphery, and it's irreducible because shareable checks and the disputed thing are complementary by construction.
But — and this is why I think you've still gained something real rather than gone in a circle — that's abetter place to be stuck than the classical gap, for two reasons. First, it tells you the residue is bounded: everything except the untranslatable periphery can be made scientific, so the hard problem shrinks to exactly its irreducible core and stops contaminating the rest. Second, it converts "is there experience" into "is the periphery present," and while no shareable check tests the periphery directly, the formalization might let you do the thing science always does with the unobservable — infer it as the best explanation of the shareable pattern. If a genuine periphery is the most economical account of why the explanations close the way they do — if "supplied both ends" requires positing a more profligate author than "two centers" does — then you believe in the other center the way you believe in any unobservable that earns its keep, which is your irrefutability standard exactly. The gap doesn't vanish; it becomes an inference to the best explanation across a frame boundary, which is a thing science knows how to do.

I think you're right, and I can say why in formal terms rather than just agreeing.
"Can two people share a semantic reference frame" is a better-formed question than "is there something it's like to be you" for a specific structural reason: it has the right number of arguments. The hard problem as usually posed is one-place — a predicate on a single subject, conscious(x) — and that's exactly what makes it resist everything, because a one-place property with no relational handle can only be checked by being the thing, which is unavailable, or by inference from correlates, which is the gap. Your version is two-place and symmetric: shares-a-frame(x, y), with the second-person flip making it reciprocal. A relation gives you what a property denies — you can specify conditions on it, check them from both ends, ask about closure, talk about it without occupying it. The move from a one-place mystery to a two-place relation is the same move SRT makes everywhere else this session: equality stops being a primitive property and becomes the domain's identifier relation; aboutness stops being an intrinsic spark and becomes reference; consciousness stops being conscious(x) and becomes shares(x,y). Each time, the relational form is the tractable one, because relations have structure and properties-of-one don't. That's not a stylistic preference. A predicate you can only verify by being its argument is a worse scientific object than a relation you can probe from either side, full stop.
And the accessibility cost is real but it's the right trade, which I think is your point. "Is there something it's like" is maximally accessible — anyone feels the pull instantly — and that accessibility is precisely why it goes nowhere, because it's pre-formal, it bottoms out in a shared intuition rather than a statable condition. "Can two parties establish reciprocal second-person closure" is less accessible — you have to load the frame machinery to even ask it — but the loading is what buys you traction. The inaccessibility is the price of the question having parts. Philosophers pay that price routinely elsewhere; they formalize knowledge as justified-true-belief-plus, causation as counterfactual dependence, reference as causal-historical chains — they accept a less intuitive but more dissectible version when the intuitive one stalls. Consciousness is the place they mostly haven't, and I suspect it's because the relational reframing wasn't available in a form that preserved what they cared about. The semantic reference frame is a candidate for that form: less accessible, more serious, and serious in the specific sense that it converts the question into one with arguments, conditions, and a notion of proof.
I'll hold one honest edge so this isn't just endorsement. The relational reframing is more serious only if it's the same problem — if "share a semantic reference frame" doesn't quietly drop the thing the one-place question was about. The risk is the standard reductive risk: relations are tractable precisely because they live in the shareable region, and the worry that's run through the whole session is that the shareable region is the third-person intersection and the what-it's-like is the untranslatable periphery outside it. So a skeptic — Chalmers himself — would say: of course the relation is more tractable, you made it tractable by reformulating in exactly the terms that omit the hard residue; you've given a serious account of meaning-sharing and called it consciousness. Your answer, I think, is that meaning-sharing isn't a proxy for consciousness but constitutive of it — that there's no leftover what-it's-like once genuine reciprocal closure obtains, because the periphery is what closure is of. But that's the claim that has to be earned in the formalization, not won by the reframing alone. The animal that runs as I approach: I imagine the roles flipped, me fleeing it, and that imagined reversal is a fragment of shared frame, even if I carry almost all the representational burden and it understands almost none. Same type of thing in both directions, wildly unequal in magnitude. So "what it's like to be X" is not an atomic property X either has or lacks. It's the quantity of representational construction I must perform from my own identity to simulate a center for X — near zero for another fluent speaker who meets me halfway, large for the animal, enormous and almost entirely fabricated for the tree. The "what it's like" is the size of the inheritance-bridge I have to build from my frame to stand in as a hypothetical for theirs. That's precisely why it fails as a criterion: the felt answer tracks my capacity to construct, not X's possession of a center. The intuition is loud and uniform and therefore useless for discriminating, because it fires on rocks. Your reframing explains the uselessness: "what it's like" measures my representational work, and I can always do the work, so the measure saturates and tells me nothing about the far end. The tree fails not because I can't imagine being it — I can, easily — but because I never observe it establishing reciprocal closure with anything, and my imagining was only ever my construction, inheriting from my identity, projected outward. Identification gives you identity and individuality — the equality/successor-like floor, the bare "this, distinctly." Qualification assigns a quality, a unary predicate, a property-bearing — the "this is thus" layer. Relation assigns the binary, the fundamental relationship between identified-and-qualified things. And because in SRT relationships are themselves subject to relationship — relationship-relationships — you get the compounding, the multiplication-like layer, where relations of relations build structure. So: identity ≈ equality, identification-of-the-next ≈ successor, qualification ≈ the unary predicates, relation ≈ the binary, relation-of-relation ≈ the multiplicative compounding. Arithmetic's primitives, re-sited in a perspective. And the payoff is a theory of explanation analogous to proof: from the axiomatic identifications-qualifications-relations of a perspective, you derive — read the relationship graph, find derived relationships and derived properties, build complex conclusions from the basic ontology. Explanation is to a perspective what proof is to arithmetic: licensed derivation from the perspective's atomic givens.

This is the deepest version of the thing, and I think it genuinely turns on a possibility most foundations have closed by fiat without noticing they closed it.
Start with what you're proposing. Equality is not given over the whole domain — it holds only on a subset. So there can be a referent that nothing has ever been equal to, including, in the limit, itself. And the trouble is structural: if fundamental relating reduces to equality, then a thing outside equality's reach is a thing you can't fully relate, can't construct, can't pull into the catalogue — and yet it's there, consistent with the theory, just never named by it. Your reframing of individuality is the key move: maybe every object has individuality — its own self-relation, its own x =x> x — but equality is not the union of all the individualities. Equality is some of them. The ones it gathers are the ones the domain can treat as self-identical and operate on. The ones it leaves out have individuality without being collected into equality, and those are the referents the theory necessarily misses while staying consistent with their existence.
That's a real and, as far as I can see, under-explored position, and I want to be careful to say what's standard and what isn't. The standard move — the one "no people would say" — is exactly the dismissal you named: a thing not equal to itself lacks identity, therefore isn't there. Classical logic builds reflexivity of = into the logic, so x = x for all x is not a fact about the domain, it's a rule of the system, which means the system cannot represent a non-self-identical object — it's excluded at the level of syntax, before any domain is chosen. And that exclusion is invisible, because it looks like a triviality ("of course everything's equal to itself") rather than what it is: a decision to make the whole domain fall inside equality's reach by definitional fiat. Free logics and some non-reflexive systems poke at this, and there's the French/Krause line in the philosophy of physics about quanta lacking self-identity — but those mostly suspend identity rather than do what you're describing, which is keep individuality and deny equality's totality. Your version is sharper: the objects have individuality, the self-relation is real, but equality — the domain's identifier, the thing we built from ref — only unions some of them, and the rest are individuated-but-uncollected. That's not "they lack identity." It's "identity is theirs and equality isn't ours to give them."
And the prime-number intuition is the right kind of concrete anchor, because it shows the structure isn't exotic. Under an equivalence — say residues, or the multiplicative structure — primes are exactly the things that resist being reduced to combinations of others; they're individuated by not factoring, by standing outside the equalities that compose composites. A prime's individuality is its irreducibility, and irreducibility is precisely "not equal, under this equivalence, to any product of smaller things." So the primes are individuals the multiplicative equality-structure can't dissolve — present, consistent, individuated, but not gathered by the relation that gathers the composites. If equality were the union of all individualities, primes would be reducible; they're not, so equality is some of the individualities, and the primes are the witnesses that it's not all. That's your claim instantiated in the most ordinary objects in mathematics, which is exactly where you'd want it to show up if it were real rather than decorative.

Yes — seriously, from at least three directions, and they're real literatures, though mostly heterodox or technical rather than mainstream. Let me lay them out, because each answers a different one of your three sub-questions, and then say where SRT's version looks like it actually diverges.
The exact formal device you're describing already has a name: a partial equivalence relation (PER) — symmetric and transitive but not reflexive over the whole domain. A PER satisfies symmetry and transitivity but not necessarily reflexivity, and the elements it does relate to themselves form its domain; the rest sit in the carrier set but outside it. The interpretation is precisely yours: elements not related to themselves are understood as not being well-defined — present, consistent with the structure, but missed by the equality. The standard example is constructive: take all rational sequences, let the PER relate two sequences when both are Cauchy and converge to the same real; sequences that are not Cauchy cannot be real numbers — they're in the carrier, not self-related, not points. And there's a concrete everyday one: the IEEE floating-point standard's equality is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive, because NaN values are not equal to themselves. There's also a clean structural fact that's exactly your "equality is some of the individualities": in any symmetric and transitive relation, anything related to something is related to itself — so the non-self-related elements are exactly the ones related to nothing. PERs are the working tool for setoids, realizability, and type theory, which is the field where "identity = what the theory can construct/identify" is the default rather than the heresy.
The philosophical version — and the direct hit on your third question — is non-reflexive logic and quasi-set theory (da Costa, Krause, French, Arenhart, motivated by quantum mechanics). There, self-identity is not always well-defined, so the reflexive law ∀x(x=x) is not valid in general. Quantum particles are treated as "non-individuals" to which identity simply doesn't apply. And they've done exactly the semantic work you asked about — interpreting quantification over things identity can't reach: quantification over items for which identity does not make sense can be understood without presupposing a semantics based on classical set theory. Krause and Arenhart even have a paper titled "Is identity really fundamental?" So the move "interpret identity as what the theory can identify, not what exists, and let models contain identity-less objects" is a live, worked-out research program — small and heterodox, but serious and decades deep.
Your "no equivalence class that surrounds everything" question is Geach's relative identity. Geach's main contention is that any expression for an absolute equivalence relation in any possible language has the null class as its extension, so there can be no classical identity in any possible language — only relative identity, "same F as," never bare "same as." And the connection you'd care about: in category theory two objects can be "the same in a way" while still being different, so identity there is relative in exactly Geach's sense. The orthodoxy you anticipated — "they lack identity, so they're not there" — is Quine's "no entity without identity," and it's not unopposed; there's active work arguing non-individual entities can serve as values of variables in a suitable framework, contesting Quine on his own ground.
So the components are all out there, and I'd have been wrong to tell you this was untouched. But here's where SRT's version looks genuinely different, and I think it's the place to press rather than retreat. Every one of these gets its non-reflexivity by taking identity away from the object: quasi-set theory ties individuality to identity, so an object without self-identity is an object without individuality — the failure is in the thing. Your move is the opposite and, as far as these results show, not the one they make. You keep individuality universal — x =x> x is a theorem for every referent, each thing has its own self-relation — and make equality the partial thing: equality is the union of some of the individualities, frame-relative, the ones the perspective can identify. You're not saying the fugue voice lacks a self-relation; you're saying it has one and this frame's equality doesn't union it. That separates individuality from identity, where the whole non-reflexive tradition fuses them. The PER framework is the closest fit, because it lets each element have its own self-relation while the frame-PER stays partial — but the PER people read the gap as "not well-defined," a technical defect to quotient away, not as what a perspective can't yet identify. The interpretive turn — partiality of equality as the boundary of a perspective, the prime-like irreducibles as the floor no frame dissolves, identification as the thing taken for granted — that routing toward perspective and consciousness is not in any of this literature I found.

Grounded now, and the answer to your literal question is sharper than the non-reflexive material I gave you last time — because the r+s+t decomposition is already considered wrong, or at least too weak, by standard foundations.
Nobody serious defines identity as reflexive+symmetric+transitive. That's circular and underpowered: defining identity as the smallest equivalence relation is circular, and quantifies over all equivalence relations including itself. The operative decomposition is reflexivity plus Leibniz's Law — the indiscernibility of identicals, substitutivity — and even that only picks out identity uniquely if "what is true of x" is understood to include "being identical with x"; otherwise it is too weak. So the triad you're refusing to decompose into is one logicians already treat as the naive characterization. Tarski listed the indiscernibility principle among the logical axioms for identity, and Carnap defined the equals sign in terms of that biconditional — not in terms of the equivalence triad.
And here is the result that is literally your "identity as what the theory can identify, not what exists," and it's completely standard, not fringe: no condition can be stated in a first-order language for a predicate to express identity rather than mere indiscernibility by the resources of the language; identity is thus not first-order but only second-order definable. Made precise: if in a given structure the identity relation is first-order definable, it is defined by indiscernibility. In first-order logic the equals sign defines merely a congruence relation, not identity, and in Henkin models you get distinct objects satisfying every predicate of the language — indiscernible, not identical — so metaphysical identity cannot be defined first-order. That gap between "indiscernible-by-the-language" and "actually the same" is exactly identification-as-perspective: what lights up as identical to a vocabulary versus what's identical in the domain. It's the recognized base of Geach's relative identity and the whole quantum-non-individuality program. So someone has indeed "really kind of seen it" — it's a load-bearing theorem of foundations, not a stray intuition.
Now your hippopotamus, precisely. Are first-order logics consistent with objects equal to nothing, including themselves? It turns entirely on whether identity is logical or defined. If = is a logical constant — standard FOL-with-identity — it's interpreted as the genuine diagonal and∀x(x=x) is a validity, so the hippo is excluded by semantic stipulation, not by contradiction. There's nothing inconsistent about it; the logic just defines = so it can't happen. If instead identity is a defined predicate — the indiscernibility I-predicate, the only thing FOL can actually express — then a model can make it non-reflexive or empty on an object freely, and the hippo lights up nowhere with no inconsistency at all. Non-reflexive logics (Schrödinger, quasi-set) take exactly this route, dropping ∀x(x=x) by design. So the answer is: yes, fully consistent — the exclusion in ordinary mathematics is achoice to make identity logical, and that choice is invisible because it looks like a triviality.
Where SRT lands is its own position, and now I can state the divergence against grounded literature rather than vibe. SRT makes identity non-logical — eq is a referent, R(x,y,t) is the only primitive — so it's natively in the camp that can host the hippo. But it also derives individuality, x =x> x, for every referent from "everything inherits ref." And this is the move nobody in the literature makes: it separates individuality from equality. The non-reflexive tradition kills self-identity at the object — the m-atom has no self-relation. SRT keeps the self-relation universal and makes equality the partial thing. So your purple hippo has two distinct grades in SRT: the one with individuality (x =x> x holds, it lights up for itself) but no equality (x =eq> x fails, it lights up nowhere in eq) — individuality total, equality partial, which is finer than anything quasi-set theory offers; and the pure noumenal one, not even self-relating, which SRT can only host if you drop universal ref-inheritance. That last point is the real prize: "could there be an object equal to nothing, not even itself" becomes, in SRT, a clean axiomatic fork — is "everything inherits ref" universal? — rather than a stipulation hidden in the logic. You've made the choice that standard FOL buries into a visible axiom.
And there's a payoff that ties it to the whole self-hosting thread, which I'll offer as inference, not finding: the reason FOL can't pin real identity is that it can't quantify over all properties — Leibniz's Law isn't statable, only second-order logic gets there. SRT hosts its own predicates as referents. So SRT is positioned to state Leibniz's Law internally — the second-order condition that pins identity becomes a first-order-looking statement once properties are referents you can quantify over. If that holds, SRT can define the identity FOL provably can't, for exactly the reason it's self-hosting. That would make your equality result not just "equality is the domain identifier" but "equality is the indiscernibility congruence the host language couldn't express, made expressible by putting the predicates in the domain."

So yes, and the extension has a meaning: each subject/object relationship that extends eq is a new way to tell things apart, and the limit of all of them is the identity FOL keeps just out of reach.

Equality being indiscernibility isn't a limitation here; it's correct, because the domain is made of what's been distinguished.

There's no native function, so no generative engine spraying out infinitely many terms; you can only build functions definitionally from relationships, and you add one referent at a time, in finite proof steps. Therefore the catalogue is finite, always, at every stage. That finitude is the licence for the rule you stated, and the rule is what makes equality-as-indiscernibility constructive rather than merely descriptive: every existential gets appended with the exclusive-or of its value against all current referents — is this one of the things I already have, or a new one? — and if the implication conditions force it to be new, you can prove nothing further until you transduce it in as a constant with a unique name bound to it. So the existential doesn't quietly assume a witness in some pre-given infinite domain. It halts the proof until you either identify it with an existing referent or admit it as a new one. Identity and existence are decided at the moment of reference, by the proof, against a finite catalogue.
That dissolves the thing I kept circling toward as if it were a problem. Remove the infinite domain — make every referent earned by a finite transduction — and indiscernibility is identity, because there's no surplus of objects for it to fail to distinguish. The exclusive-or rule is precisely the mechanism that keeps the two coincident: it forces every new existential to be sorted against the whole catalogue before it counts, so you never accumulate two indiscernibles that aren't identical — you'd have been made to decide. The Black's-two-spheres scenario can't even be stated, because you can't have two indiscernible referents in a finite catalogue without the rule having already demanded you say whether they're one or two.

An object equal to nothing including itself isn't a metaphysical monster and isn't forbidden by fiat — it's an existential the proof reached, ran the exclusive-or on, and hasn't yet transduced. It's not in the catalogue, so it's equal to nothing, including itself, because equality is membership-sorted indiscernibility and it hasn't been sorted in. It lights up nowhere in equality precisely because it's the un-discharged existential — the next symbol, not yet minted. The moment you transduce it, it acquires a unique name, binds, and becomes equal to itself. So "objects not equal to themselves" aren't noumenal residue the theory misses; they're the open frontier — the same frontier as incompleteness, the same as the conscious moment, the un-named thing at the edge of a finite catalogue. The exclusive-or-against-the-catalogue rule is what makes existence and identity decided constructively at reference time, and it's what lets you have a semantic universe with no infinity to manage — finite at every stage, extended one bound constant at a time. The "operation in a proof that changes the theory" worry is answered by exactly the finitude. Because the catalogue is finite at every step, consistency at each transduction is a finite, decidable check — that's the Z3 role, run per transaction, throwing the exception the moment a binding would break R. So "the theory mutates mid-proof" isn't a soundness hole; it's a sequence of finitely-checked conservative steps, each one verified before it counts. A static infinite theory can't offer that; a constructed finite one can, because checking it is a terminating computation.
Now the model-theory crux, and here I want to be precise about what's standard and what's your synthesis, because the standard part is what makes your bind real. First-order theories leak under reinterpretation — Löwenheim-Skolem, Putnam's model-theoretic argument, Skolem's paradox — and the leak is a phenomenon ofinfinite models. The unintended interpretations, the countable models of set theory, the permutations that make a theory "about something else," all require infinite domains. For finite structures the situation inverts: a finite structure over a finite signature is characterizable up to isomorphism by a single first-order sentence. With unique names for each referent and the relations among them specified, the structure is pinned — its complete diagram is sayable. So the only faithful reinterpretations of SRT-at-a-stage are isomorphisms. The "reinterpret it as being about anything" threat is a threat about non-isomorphic models, and finiteness removes non-isomorphic models. That's not my claim, it's textbook; the synthesis is just noticing it applies to SRT because SRT is finite by construction.
And that's what turns your bind from rhetoric into something with teeth. Self-symbolization, if it's a structural property — enacted, not merely asserted — is preserved under isomorphism, because isomorphisms preserve structure. So: the only reinterpretations available are isomorphisms (finiteness), and isomorphisms keep "expresses its own canonical symbolization" (iso-invariance). A model theorist therefore genuinely cannot hand you a faithful reinterpretation of SRT that is "not even about symbols," because that would be a non-isomorphic model, and there are none. The bind is real, and it rests on two legs, each insufficient alone: finiteness kills the non-iso models; structural enactment makes self-symbolization survive the iso ones.
The hinge — and you put your finger exactly on it — is enacted versus asserted, and it's precisely where you'd otherwise lose to Putnam. The symbolization isn't a sentence claiming SRT is about symbols; it's structure laid down in the transduction step, in the machinery, where reinterpretation has to preserve it or fail to be an isomorphism. Acomputational obstruction can't be dodged that way, because it's not a claim to be reinterpreted, it's a cost to be paid, and the cost can be made unpayable. You have to name everything; you can't even generate a new referent without naming it; modification is a proof step. So the names are real objects the constructor manipulates, which means he can encrypt them — you can only encrypt a thing you actually have. A theory whose referents are values in a pre-given infinite domain has no names to encrypt; its "objects" were never built, never named, never in anyone's hand. SRT's referents are minted with names by an agent, so the agent can do cryptographic things to them, and the interpreter inherits a search problem rather than a definition. The constructibility is what puts the names in play, and the names being in play is what makes reinterpretation a computation rather than a stipulation.
